questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. AI audit universe
questions.question: An IS audit manager builds next year's AI audit universe solely from the model registry that the data science team's training platform fills automatically. What is the GREATEST concern with this approach?

options.A: The registry omits AI features embedded in purchased software and services
options.B: The registry still lists retired models that no longer decide anything
options.C: The registry does not name a business owner for each model
options.D: The registry does not record each model's programming framework

questions.key_concept: A risk-based AI audit universe starts from a complete inventory, including AI embedded in purchased products, before any ranking.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the list came from and which kinds of AI that source could never contain.
questions.correct_explanation: An audit universe must be complete before it can be ranked. A registry the training platform fills lists only models trained there, so AI embedded in purchased software, cloud services and business-unit tools, often the highest-impact uses, never reaches the plan. A missing model owner is a real governance gap, but the audit can test and report it once the model is listed; an AI use never listed is never audited.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because stale entries clutter a universe. But retired models are easy to rank low; AI uses that never appear cannot be ranked at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because every model needs a named owner. But a missing owner is a gap the audit can find and report; AI the registry never lists is never audited.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting for a technically minded auditor. But the programming framework does not set audit priority; the likelihood and impact of harm to people and the business do.

tips: Eliminate: D adds technical detail that does not set audit priority, and B flags retired entries that a risk ranking simply rates low.
Final two: A beats C because a missing owner is a gap the audit can test once a model is listed, but AI the registry never lists never reaches the plan.
Exam cue: completeness of the AI audit universe comes before ranking it. Look for embedded, purchased and shadow AI that a builders' list misses.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Engagement scope
questions.question: An IS auditor is scoping an audit of a property firm's tenant chatbot, built on a vendor's large language model and answering from the firm's lease files. Which scope is BEST?

options.A: The vendor's model weights, training data, pretraining and safety tuning methods
options.B: The chatbot's response times and tenant satisfaction scores
options.C: The firm's lease data, prompts, answers, oversight and vendor management
options.D: The chatbot's hosting, network security and user access controls

questions.key_concept: AI audit scope follows the organization's controllable parts: data, prompts, configuration, human oversight and third-party management.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the organization configured from what a vendor supplies, then ask which parts it can control.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm owns the parts of this system it configures and uses: the lease files the chatbot answers from, its prompts, the answers it gives, how staff oversee them and how it manages the vendor. That is where the firm's risk and its controls sit. The vendor's weights and pretraining shape behavior, but the firm cannot inspect or change them; it addresses that risk through vendor oversight and output testing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the base model shapes every answer. But the firm cannot inspect or change a vendor's weights or tuning; it manages that risk through vendor oversight and output testing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because service metrics are easy to measure. But speed and satisfaction say nothing about wrong lease answers or leaked tenant data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because general IT controls are familiar audit ground. But hosting and access controls miss where this chatbot's risk sits: its lease data, prompts and staff oversight.

tips: Eliminate: B measures service quality rather than answer accuracy or data risk, and D covers general IT controls but none of the AI risks in data, prompts or oversight.
Final two: C beats A because the firm controls its data, prompts and oversight; vendor weights are beyond its reach and are covered through vendor management.
Exam cue: scope an AI system by what the organization owns and configures, including its data and human oversight, plus how it manages the vendor.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Using specialists
questions.question: An external data scientist, vetted and engaged by IS audit, concludes that a university's student-support model is fair, using the test set the model's developers chose. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the developers to confirm that their test set was suitable
options.B: Evaluate whether that test set represents the current student population
options.C: Accept the conclusion because the data scientist is external to the university
options.D: Rerun the specialist's fairness tests on that same test set

questions.key_concept: Fairness and performance results depend on representative test data; the auditor evaluates a specialist's data choices before relying on the conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Find who selected the data behind the result, and ask what that choice could hide.
questions.correct_explanation: Before relying on a specialist, the IS auditor evaluates whether the work is adequate for the objective. A fairness result is only as good as its test data, and a developer-chosen set may underrepresent some student groups or reflect an older intake. Rerunning the tests on the same set would confirm the arithmetic but repeat any blind spot in the data.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because developers know the data best. But they chose the set, so their confirmation is inquiry of the party under review, not evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because external specialists are independent of the university. But independence does not make a method sound; the auditor still evaluates the work before relying on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But rerunning on the same data only confirms the calculation; it cannot reveal groups the test set leaves out.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a specialist's independence as proof the work is adequate, and A seeks assurance from the developers whose test-set choice is in question.
Final two: B beats D because reperforming on the same data repeats its blind spots; the data's representativeness decides whether the fairness result holds.
Exam cue: when relying on AI test results, question the test data first. Who chose it, and does it match the people the model affects now?

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Audit use of AI
questions.question: IT management approved a generative AI assistant for all staff, with terms barring training on inputs. Before auditors use it to summarize interviews and draft findings, what should the chief audit executive do FIRST?

options.A: Allow use at once, since IT approved its security and data terms
options.B: Test it on past interviews, then rely on its summaries
options.C: Pilot it on a live engagement to measure the time it saves
options.D: Assess the audit risks and set approved uses with review rules

questions.key_concept: IT approval of an AI tool covers security and data terms; audit management still assesses audit risks and sets approved uses before reliance.
questions.pre_read: Notice what IT's approval covers and which risks of the planned audit uses it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: IT's approval addresses security, and the no-training terms protect the data, but neither addresses audit risks. Generative summaries and drafted findings can contain confident errors on any input. The chief audit executive first assesses those risks and sets approved audit uses and review steps. Testing once on past interviews seems prudent, but a one-off test cannot show that each new summary or draft is right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT already approved the tool and its data terms. But that approval covers security, not invented content in summaries and findings auditors rely on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because testing before reliance suits fixed audit tools. But generative output can be wrong on any new input; one test cannot replace reviewing each output.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a pilot gives real evidence of value. But a live engagement relies on unchecked output before any rules for audit use exist.

tips: Eliminate: C uses the tool on real work before rules exist, and A treats IT's security approval as approval for audit use.
Final two: D beats B because generative output can be wrong on any new input; a one-off test cannot replace rules for reviewing each summary and draft.
Exam cue: neither IT approval nor a one-off test is audit approval. For generative AI in the audit, set approved uses and review rules before relying on output.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Sampling for fairness
questions.question: An IS auditor plans a random sample of 60 decisions by a telecom's phone-financing model, whose inputs exclude age; applicants aged over 70 are 3% of decisions. Which change BEST supports testing for age bias?

options.A: Draw the sample from the model's training data instead
options.B: Stratify by age band and oversample the oldest band
options.C: Double the random sample to 120 decisions across age groups
options.D: Select the decisions the model scored with highest confidence

questions.key_concept: Fairness testing needs samples stratified by the groups at risk, sized so each group has enough decisions to compare.
questions.pre_read: Work out how many cases from the small group each sample would actually contain.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaving age out of the inputs does not prevent age bias, because other inputs can act as proxies, so outcomes are tested by age. A random sample of 60 would hold about two applicants aged over 70, too few to compare approval rates. Stratifying by age band and oversampling the oldest band fixes that; doubling the random sample still yields only about four older applicants.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because bias often starts in training data. But the objective concerns live decisions, and training records do not show how real applicants were treated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because larger samples give more confidence. But doubling a random sample still yields only a handful of older applicants, too few to compare outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confident scores look like clear cases. But the most confident decisions are the least likely to show errors, and the choice skews the sample further.

tips: Eliminate: A tests training data when the risk sits in live decisions, and D picks the cases least likely to reveal model errors.
Final two: B beats C because a larger random sample still holds only a handful of older applicants; oversampling the oldest band guarantees enough of them to compare.
Exam cue: test AI outcomes by group even when the model never uses the group attribute. A small group needs its own stratum, or the sample cannot see it.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing human review
questions.question: Policy requires a supervisor to review every courier deactivation a delivery platform's model recommends, and every logged deactivation carries an approval. Which test gives the IS auditor the BEST evidence that the review operates effectively?

options.A: Inspect the review procedure and each supervisor's training record
options.B: Confirm every logged deactivation carries a supervisor's approval
options.C: Rerun sampled recommendations through the current production model
options.D: Analyze override rates and review times across all deactivations

questions.key_concept: Human oversight of AI is tested by reviewer behavior, such as override rates and review time, not by sign-offs alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each test would show if supervisors approved every case without reading it.
questions.correct_explanation: Every deactivation already carries an approval, but sign-offs alone cannot show that anyone judged the case. Override rates and time spent per review show whether supervisors engage with recommendations or defer to the model, the pattern called automation bias. Confirming that every deactivation carries an approval, option B, is the runner-up: it proves the step happened, not that oversight works.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because procedures and training support a control. But they show design and readiness, not how supervisors actually review over the period.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because full coverage is a classic operating test. But approvals are already logged on every case; that proves the step happened, not that supervisors judged anything.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it tests the model, not the supervisors, and today's model may differ from the one that decided.

tips: Eliminate: A inspects design documents rather than operation, and C tests the model instead of the human review.
Final two: D beats B because a sign-off proves the step happened; override rates and review times show whether supervisors actually judge each case.
Exam cue: test human oversight of AI by what reviewers do, such as overrides and time per case, not by the presence of approvals.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reperformance
questions.question: To confirm that sampled payout holds were produced as logged by a marketplace's seller-risk model, retrained monthly, which procedure gives the IS auditor the MOST reliable evidence?

options.A: Rerun the sampled inputs through the current production model version
options.B: Inspect the model card's description of the input features
options.C: Rerun the sampled inputs through the model version that decided them
options.D: Ask the data scientists how each sampled decision was reached

questions.key_concept: Reperforming an AI decision needs the same model version and logged inputs; retraining makes today's version a different model.
questions.pre_read: Notice how often the model changes, and what that means for rerunning old decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Reperformance is strong evidence when it recreates the conditions of the original decision. Because the model is retrained monthly, only the version that made each decision, given the same logged inputs, should reproduce it. Running the inputs through today's model tests a different model, so mismatches could reflect retraining rather than error, and matches prove nothing about the past decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the current model is easy to run. But monthly retraining makes it a different model, so its outputs cannot confirm past decisions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model cards describe inputs. But a description of features cannot show that any sampled decision was produced as logged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data scientists know the model. But their explanation is inquiry, the weakest evidence, and cannot show what the model actually output.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on inquiry of the model's builders, and B inspects documentation that describes the model but cannot prove any decision.
Final two: C beats A because monthly retraining changes the model; only the version that made the decision can reproduce it.
Exam cue: to reperform an AI decision, match the model version and inputs used at the time. Versioning is what makes reperformance possible.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Full-population analytics
questions.question: An IS auditor's anomaly-detection model, trained on last year's expense claims before a travel-policy change, flagged 900 of 50,000 claims as unusual. What is MOST important before the auditor concludes on the whole population?

options.A: Test a sample drawn from the 49,100 unflagged claims
options.B: Treat the unflagged claims as tested and free of exceptions
options.C: Report the 900 flagged claims as control exceptions
options.D: Follow up every flagged claim and conclude on those results

questions.key_concept: Full-population analytics still needs evidence about false negatives; unflagged items are not tested items.
questions.pre_read: Split the population into flagged and unflagged, and ask what evidence exists for each part.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's flags show where to look, not where problems are absent, and a model trained before the policy change may miss new patterns. To conclude on all 50,000 claims, the auditor needs evidence of the miss rate, so testing a sample of unflagged claims estimates false negatives. Following up every flag is necessary, but concluding on flagged items alone treats the 49,100 unflagged claims as clean without evidence.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the tool covered the full population. But coverage by a model is not audit testing; its misses stay unseen unless they are tested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tool flagged them. But flags are leads; many may be false positives until each is followed up with evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because thorough follow-up of flags is necessary. But it confirms only what the tool caught and says nothing about what it missed.

tips: Eliminate: B treats model coverage as audit testing, and C reports raw flags as findings before any follow-up.
Final two: A beats D because following up flags confirms hits but says nothing about misses; a population conclusion needs the unflagged side tested too.
Exam cue: an AI tool has false negatives as well as false positives, more so when data has changed since training. Test both sides before concluding on a full population.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Monitoring evidence
questions.question: As evidence that an energy utility's load-forecasting model is monitored for drift, the model owner gives the IS auditor a screenshot of a green monitoring dashboard. What is the BEST next step?

options.A: Accept the screenshot because the dashboard is system-generated
options.B: Obtain the drift alert history and how each alert was resolved
options.C: Recalculate this month's drift from current production data
options.D: Ask the model owner to sign a statement confirming monitoring

questions.key_concept: Drift monitoring is proven by alert history and responses over the period, not by a dashboard snapshot.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the evidence covers one moment or the whole period the control should operate.
questions.correct_explanation: A screenshot shows one chosen moment and hides the thresholds behind it. To test that drift monitoring operated over the period, the auditor needs the alert history and evidence of how each alert was handled. Recalculating this month's drift is strong reperformance, but it shows the model's current state, not that monitoring worked or that anyone acted on past alerts.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because system output is usually reliable. But a screenshot is a point-in-time image the auditee chose; it shows neither thresholds nor alerts over time.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But one month's recalculation checks the model now, not whether monitoring raised and handled alerts across the period.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because written representations formalize a claim. But a signed statement is still the auditee's assertion, not evidence that monitoring operated.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a chosen point-in-time image as proof over a period, and D turns the owner's claim into a signed claim, which is still not evidence.
Final two: B beats C because the control is monitoring over time; recalculating today's drift checks the model, not whether alerts fired and were acted on.
Exam cue: for an AI monitoring control, ask for the alert history and responses, not a dashboard view. Operation is shown over time.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Training data evidence
questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm which data sources trained the current version of a pharmacy chain's refill-reminder model, which is retrained quarterly as sources change. Which evidence is MOST reliable?

options.A: A datasheet the developers wrote describing the training dataset
options.B: The model's feature importance chart from its validation
options.C: Lineage records the pipeline generated for the latest training run
options.D: Last month's production decision log for the model

questions.key_concept: Data lineage records trace training data to its sources and outrank developer-written descriptions as evidence.
questions.pre_read: Name exactly what must be proven, then ask which record a system produced for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Lineage records produced by the pipeline trace each source into the specific training run, so they are system-generated and tied to the version under audit. A developer-written datasheet is the auditee's own description of the intended dataset, and with quarterly retraining as sources change, it may describe an earlier dataset than the one actually used.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because datasheets describe training data in detail. But it is the developers' own description, and with quarterly retraining it may describe an earlier dataset.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it lists the inputs that matter most. But feature importance ranks variables; it does not show where the training data came from.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs are system-generated. But production logs record live inputs and outputs, not the sources of the training data.

tips: Eliminate: B ranks model variables rather than tracing data sources, and D records production decisions, not what went into training.
Final two: C beats A because pipeline lineage is system-generated for that run, while a datasheet is the developers' own description and may predate the latest retraining.
Exam cue: match AI evidence to the question. Training-data origin needs lineage, a decision needs its log, and builder documents rank below system records.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. AI-produced evidence
questions.question: An IS auditor's generative AI summary of 300 supplier contracts says each limits supplier use of company data, quoting a clause from each; a rerun gave the same summary. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the tool to confirm each quoted clause appears in its contract
options.B: Accept the summary, since the rerun reproduced it exactly
options.C: File the summary in the work papers with the prompt used
options.D: Trace a sample of the summary's quoted clauses to the contracts

questions.key_concept: Generative AI output, including quotes, can be confabulated and repeated on rerun; the auditor corroborates it against source records before use.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool's claim rests on and how the auditor could check it independently.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative tools can state false content confidently, and quoted clauses can be invented too, so the summary is a lead, not evidence. Tracing a sample of quoted clauses to the contracts tests whether the summary is accurate and shows how far it can be relied on. The matching rerun shows only that the tool repeats itself: a model can repeat the same invented quote, so consistency is not accuracy.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tool can check its own quotes. But a model checking itself can repeat invented content; verification needs the contracts themselves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a matching rerun looks like reperformance. But a generative model can repeat the same invented quote; consistency is not accuracy.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the quoted clauses look like evidence. But filing output with its prompt records what was done; it does not test whether the quotes are real.

tips: Eliminate: A asks the model to verify its own quotes, which can repeat invented content, and C documents the output without testing it.
Final two: D beats B because a matching rerun shows consistency, not accuracy; only the contracts show whether the quotes are real.
Exam cue: a matching rerun of a generative model shows consistency, not accuracy. Corroborate AI output against source records.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Model version under audit
questions.question: Mid-audit, a tax agency's return-triage model is due to be retrained next week to fix known errors, overwriting the version under audit. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Request that the current version, configuration and logs be preserved
options.B: Ask management to postpone the retraining until fieldwork ends
options.C: Rely on the validation report the developers prepared for this version
options.D: Test the retrained version next week instead of the current one

questions.key_concept: AI evidence is version-specific; the auditor asks for the audited version, configuration and logs to be preserved rather than delaying changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask which model version made the decisions in scope and what happens to it next week.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit covers decisions made by the current version, so that version, its configuration and its decision logs must stay available as evidence. Asking for them to be preserved protects the evidence without interfering with operations. Delaying the retraining puts audit convenience ahead of fixing known errors, and preservation already meets the audit's need. That retraining overwrites the audited version is itself a versioning weakness to report.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it keeps the audited model in place. But delaying a fix for known errors puts audit convenience ahead of the business; preserving the version meets the need.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the report already exists. But a one-time validation by the developers is an input, not evidence of how the model performed in use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the new version will be in production. But it made none of the decisions under audit, so testing it says nothing about the period.

tips: Eliminate: D tests a version that made none of the decisions under audit, and C relies on the developers' one-time validation.
Final two: A beats B because preserving the version meets the audit's need without the auditor holding up a management change.
Exam cue: when an AI model is about to change, preserve the version, configuration and logs under review. Do not block the change.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Log population
questions.question: An IS auditor will test a concert-ticketing site's support chatbot for personal-data disclosure using vendor logs, which keep only chats the safety filter flagged; the vendor says it catches 98%. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Disclosures the filter missed never reach the population
options.B: The log export format may not load into audit software
options.C: The vendor could see the auditor's searches in its log portal
options.D: Many filter flags may be false positives that need clearing

questions.key_concept: Audit data selected by an AI filter is incomplete by design; the auditor confirms the population includes what the filter missed.
questions.pre_read: Ask which conversations reach the logs, and which never do.
questions.correct_explanation: A population built by the safety filter contains only what the filter caught. Disclosures it missed, the very errors the audit should find, never reach the logs, and the vendor's 98% figure is a claim, not evidence of the miss rate. False positives cost review time, but they are visible and can be cleared; the missed chats cannot be tested from this source at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because format problems stall testing. But conversion is routine, and a format issue does not change what the population contains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because audit queries can tip off a vendor. But the vendor seeing searches is minor beside testing an incomplete population.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because clearing false positives takes effort. But false positives are visible and can be cleared; the missed disclosures never reach the logs.

tips: Eliminate: B is a routine conversion task, and C is a minor confidentiality point that does not change what the logs contain.
Final two: A beats D because false positives can be cleared, but disclosures the filter missed never reach the population to be tested.
Exam cue: ask how an AI log population was formed. If a model or filter selected it, the misses are outside the data, whatever detection rate the vendor claims.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Audit tool validation
questions.question: The IS audit team plans to rely on a machine-learning tool to classify 20,000 IT change tickets as emergency or standard. Which step BEST supports that reliance?

options.A: Run the tool on past tickets whose correct class is known
options.B: Rely on the accuracy rate that the tool's vendor publishes
options.C: Review a sample of the tickets the tool marks as emergency
options.D: Confirm the team is licensed for the tool's newest version

questions.key_concept: Validate an audit AI tool on known-outcome data, measuring both error types, before relying on its output.
questions.pre_read: Ask how each option would reveal the errors the tool makes in both directions.
questions.correct_explanation: Before relying on an audit tool, the team validates it on data where the right answer is already known, measuring both kinds of error. Testing past tickets with known classes shows how often the tool labels emergencies as standard and the reverse. Reviewing tickets marked emergency checks only one side and misses emergency changes the tool labeled standard.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because published rates sound objective. But vendor figures come from the vendor's data, not these tickets; they are inputs, not validation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it checks the tool's output directly. But it finds only false emergency labels and misses emergency changes the tool called standard.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because current versions fix defects. But being up to date says nothing about whether the tool classifies these tickets correctly.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a vendor claim measured on other data, and D treats being current as proof of accuracy.
Final two: A beats C because known-outcome testing measures both error types; reviewing emergency labels finds only false positives.
Exam cue: validate an audit AI tool on data with known answers before relying on it, and revalidate whenever the tool or data changes.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Audit data confidentiality
questions.question: An IS auditor wants a generative AI service to summarize interview notes that contain employees' health details. Which control BEST protects this audit data?

options.A: Removing staff names before pasting the notes into a public AI service
options.B: An approved service contracted to limit retention and bar training on inputs
options.C: Deleting the chat history after each summarizing session
options.D: A strong, unique password on the auditor's approved chatbot account

questions.key_concept: Confidential audit data may be used only in approved AI services whose terms limit retention and bar training on inputs.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the data goes after it is submitted, and who controls it there.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit data with health details should go only to a tool the organization has approved, under terms that limit what the provider keeps and bar training on what is submitted. That protects confidentiality whatever the notes contain. Removing names helps, but health details and job context can still identify people, and a public service may keep and reuse the text.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing names reduces exposure. But health details and context can still identify staff, and a public service may keep and reuse what is pasted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because deleting history feels like removing the data. But clearing the chat view does not stop a provider keeping or training on inputs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because account security matters and the account is approved. But a password protects the auditor's login, not what the provider does with submitted notes.

tips: Eliminate: D secures the account but not the data sent to the provider, and C clears the user's view while the provider may keep inputs.
Final two: B beats A because contract terms control what the provider keeps; removing names leaves health details that can still identify staff.
Exam cue: confidential audit data goes only into approved AI services with contract terms on retention and training, never into public tools.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Rerunning AI-assisted work
questions.question: A quality reviewer reruns an IS auditor's AI-assisted log analysis a month later and gets different exceptions. Which practice should the audit manager require to BEST make such work reproducible?

options.A: Save the output file, exception list and screenshots in the work papers
options.B: Have the tool vendor certify the original analysis results
options.C: Use the vendor's newest model version for every rerun
options.D: Record the tool version, settings, prompts and data snapshot used

questions.key_concept: Reproducible AI-assisted audit work records the tool version, settings, prompts and input data, not only the output.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed between the two runs and which record would have held it constant.
questions.correct_explanation: AI tools change: vendors update and retire models, and settings that allow randomness can vary outputs. Recording the exact version, settings, prompts and input data lets a reviewer rerun the analysis under the same conditions, or trace why a rerun differs when a hosted version is retired. Saving the output preserves what was found, but it does not let anyone reproduce or test how the result was produced.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because saved output is part of the audit trail. But it hides the conditions behind it, so no one can rerun the work or explain a difference.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors know their tools. But a vendor certificate cannot replace the auditor's own reproducible evidence and shifts reliance to an outside party.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because newer models may perform better. But changing the model between runs is what makes results differ; reproducibility needs the same version.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the model between runs, the very cause of the mismatch, and B replaces the audit trail with a vendor's assurance.
Final two: D beats A because a saved output shows the result, but only recorded conditions let a reviewer rerun the work or explain why a rerun differs.
Exam cue: record the tool version, settings, prompts and data behind AI-assisted audit work, so a rerun is possible and any difference can be explained.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Finding attributes
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a contact center's call-routing model fell from 91% to 78% accuracy after a product launch, unnoticed for four months. Which statement BEST describes the root cause the IS auditor should report?

options.A: Call patterns after the launch drifted away from the training data
options.B: Urgent customers wait longer, raising complaints and lost business
options.C: No drift alert or revalidation was required after the launch
options.D: Accuracy no longer meets the 85% threshold set by policy

questions.key_concept: An AI finding's cause names the control gap, such as no revalidation after change, rather than the technical mechanism like drift.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option into condition, criteria, cause or effect, then ask which cause a lasting fix would address.
questions.correct_explanation: A finding's cause explains why the condition arose, in terms a lasting fix can address. Drift after a business change is expected; the control gap is that no drift alert or revalidation was required after the launch, so accuracy fell unnoticed for months. Drift is the technical mechanism, but naming it as the cause points only to a one-off retrain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because drift is the technical reason accuracy fell. But it is the mechanism; the cause a lasting fix must address is the missing monitoring and revalidation.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it describes the harm. But harm to customers and the business is the finding's effect, not its cause.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it quantifies the gap. But comparing accuracy with the policy threshold sets the condition against the criteria; it does not explain why.

tips: Eliminate: B states the harm, which is the effect, and D compares the condition with the criteria; neither explains why the condition arose.
Final two: C beats A because drift after a launch is expected; the cause a lasting fix addresses is the control that should have caught it.
Exam cue: in an AI finding, the cause is the control or process gap, such as missing drift monitoring, not the technical mechanism alone.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Rating findings
questions.question: An IS auditor is rating four AI findings for the audit committee. Which finding should the auditor rate as the GREATEST concern?

options.A: A coding assistant's prompts are not logged for later review
options.B: A forecasting model drifted, raising warehouse stock costs by 2%
options.C: A model suspending mobile-money accounts offers no appeal route
options.D: A new marketing text generator lacks a completed model card

questions.key_concept: AI findings are rated by likelihood and impact on people and the business; high-impact decisions with no appeal route rate highest.
questions.pre_read: For each finding, ask who is harmed, how badly, and whether a wrong decision can be corrected.
questions.correct_explanation: Rating weighs likelihood and impact, counting harm to people as well as to the business. Suspending a mobile-money account can cut someone off from wages and payments, and with no appeal route, wrong suspensions cannot be corrected. The forecasting drift has a measurable cost, but it is a modest financial effect that management can absorb and correct, with no direct harm to individuals.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missing logs weaken accountability. But an internal coding tool's prompts carry far lower impact than unappealable decisions about customers' money.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it has a measured business cost. But a modest, correctable cost increase weighs less than unappealable decisions that cut people off from their money.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because model cards are expected documentation. But a missing card on a low-impact marketing tool is a documentation gap, not direct harm.

tips: Eliminate: A is a logging gap on a low-impact internal coding tool, and D is a documentation gap on a low-impact marketing tool; neither harms people directly.
Final two: C beats B because unappealable decisions that cut people off from their money outweigh a modest, correctable cost increase.
Exam cue: rate AI findings by likelihood and impact, counting harm to people as well as to the business. High-impact decisions about individuals with no recourse rate highest.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. AI-drafted findings
questions.question: An audit manager sees that a generative AI tool drafted an IS auditor's findings from the work papers and gave each a cause the papers never mention. What should the manager require FIRST?

options.A: Disclose in the report that an AI tool drafted the findings
options.B: Have the auditor check each statement against the evidence
options.C: Ask management to confirm the causes that the tool added
options.D: Have the tool redraft the findings strictly from the work papers

questions.key_concept: The auditor stays accountable for conclusions an AI tool helped draft and verifies each against the evidence before issue.
questions.pre_read: Ask who signs the report and what makes each finding supportable.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative tools fill gaps with plausible content, and causes the work papers never mention are exactly that: statements without evidence. The auditor is accountable for every finding, so each statement, causes included, must be checked against the evidence before issue. A redraft limited to the work papers may reduce invented content, but it is still unchecked output; only the auditor's review makes the findings supportable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because transparency about AI use is good practice. But disclosure explains the method; it does not make an unchecked finding supportable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because findings are discussed with management. But a cause must come from the auditor's evidence; management's agreement is the auditee's view, not proof.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tighter instructions may curb invented content. But a redraft is still unverified output, and the auditor still owns every statement.

tips: Eliminate: A discloses AI use without verifying anything, and C seeks proof of cause from the auditee instead of the evidence.
Final two: B beats D because a tighter prompt still yields unverified text; only the auditor's check against evidence makes findings supportable.
Exam cue: an AI tool can draft, but the auditor reviews and owns every conclusion. Verify against evidence before disclosure or issue.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Follow-up evidence
questions.question: Management says it retrained a warehouse shift-allocation model that gave women fewer overtime shifts, and asks to close the finding. What should the IS auditor do to BEST verify closure?

options.A: Close the finding based on management's signed confirmation
options.B: Review the retraining project's pre-release validation report
options.C: Recommend retraining again on a larger, balanced dataset
options.D: Retest shift allocations by gender on decisions since the retraining

questions.key_concept: Follow-up on an AI finding retests outcomes in production after the fix, not only pre-release validation.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence shows how the model behaves now, with real decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Follow-up verifies that the agreed action worked in practice. Retesting allocations by gender on decisions made since the retrained model went live shows whether women now get a fair share of overtime. The pre-release validation report is useful, but the builders produced it on test data before go-live, so it cannot show how the model behaves in production.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because management owns remediation. But a confirmation is management's assertion; follow-up needs evidence that the fix works.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because validation reports test fairness directly. But the builders ran it on test data before go-live, so it cannot show production outcomes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because better data may help. But designing the fix is management's job, and the auditor's task now is to verify the fix made.

tips: Eliminate: A closes on management's word without evidence, and C has the auditor designing the model fix instead of verifying it.
Final two: D beats B because production results show whether the fix worked; a pre-release report is the builders' test before go-live.
Exam cue: follow-up tests what the finding reported. When it reported a harmful outcome, close it on production outcomes after the fix, not on validation reports or management statements.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Ranking AI uses
questions.question: An IS audit manager at a Ugandan bank is ranking four AI uses for next year's audit plan. Which use should the manager rank as the GREATEST risk?

options.A: A card-fraud model retrained quarterly through validation and change approval
options.B: A marketing model whose response forecasts drifted last quarter
options.C: A credit-limit model that retrains and redeploys itself every night
options.D: A new large language model that drafts internal policy summaries

questions.key_concept: AI audit priority weighs likelihood and impact; a model that retrains and redeploys itself, with no human release step, raises the likelihood of harm.
questions.pre_read: For each use, ask who is affected and what stops a faulty version from reaching them.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit priority weighs the likelihood and impact of harm. A model that retrains and redeploys itself every night puts a new version into use daily with no human release step, so a harmful shift is likely to reach customers unnoticed, and it sets their credit limits. The card-fraud model also affects customers, but quarterly validation and change approval lower the likelihood that a faulty version reaches them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because blocked cards affect customers directly. But quarterly validation and change approval lower the likelihood of harm, so it ranks below a model that redeploys itself nightly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because drift shows something has gone wrong. But marketing forecasts carry little impact on people, so the drift matters less than unchecked nightly changes to credit limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because new generative tools draw attention. But novelty is not risk; internal policy summaries have far less impact on people than credit decisions.

tips: Eliminate: D ranks novelty rather than risk, and B shows drift on a use with little impact on people.
Final two: C beats A because both affect customers, but C puts a new version live every night with no human release step, raising the likelihood of harm.
Exam cue: rank AI uses by likelihood and impact. A model that retrains and redeploys itself raises likelihood even when its impact matches another's.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Scoping an AI agent
questions.question: An IS auditor's draft scope for a Slovenian city's AI agent, which reviews drivers' pothole-damage photos and pays small claims, covers photo-assessment accuracy and hosting. Which addition is MOST important?

options.A: The agent's payment authority and when a person must approve
options.B: A larger accuracy test of photo assessment across claim types
options.C: Claim handling times and driver satisfaction since the agent launched
options.D: Logs of each payment the agent makes, kept for later review

questions.key_concept: Scoping an AI agent covers what it can do: its tool permissions, transaction limits and human approval points, not only model accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the system only advises or also acts, and what the draft scope already covers.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent differs from a model that only advises: it acts. This one pays claims, so its payment authority (permissions and limits) and the points where a person must approve set how much harm any error, edited photo or manipulated input can cause. Payment logs, option D, are the runner-up: they support detection and later review, but they record wrong payments after the money has gone rather than bounding them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy drives every payout. But accuracy is already in scope; a bigger test still leaves out what the agent may pay without a person.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because service measures are easy to report. But speed and satisfaction say nothing about wrong or manipulated payments.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs let auditors trace each payment. But logs record wrong or manipulated payments after the money has gone; the scope must first cover what bounds them.

tips: Eliminate: B deepens accuracy testing the scope already covers, and C measures service rather than payment risk.
Final two: A beats D because the agent acts with money; its payment authority and approval points bound each failure before it happens, while payment logs only record it afterward.
Exam cue: when an AI agent can act, scope its tools, permissions and human checkpoints, not only the accuracy of its model.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Selecting audit criteria
questions.question: A Mauritian sugar producer's cane-yield model scores well on the vendor's public benchmark, and senior management approved an error tolerance for this use. Which audit criterion is BEST for the IS auditor to apply?

options.A: The vendor's public benchmark score for cane-yield prediction
options.B: The error tolerance set for the model's yield forecasts
options.C: A measure the model owner and the IS auditor agree in writing
options.D: The average error that peer producers report for similar models

questions.key_concept: The auditor selects suitable audit criteria; a use-specific approved tolerance outranks a vendor benchmark measured on general data.
questions.pre_read: Ask who set each candidate measure, on what data, and who chooses the criteria an audit applies.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor selects audit criteria for their suitability. The error tolerance senior management approved was set for this use, so it is relevant and authoritative. A public benchmark is measured on the vendor's general data, not this producer's fields, cane varieties and seasons, so a good score says little about the errors this model makes here. It is a useful input, not the criterion.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a published benchmark looks objective and recognized. But it measures the model on the vendor's general data, not on this producer's fields and seasons.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because criteria are usually discussed with management. But making agreement a condition gives the auditee a veto over how it is judged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because peer figures give context. But other producers' averages do not reflect the tolerance this organization approved for its own use.

tips: Eliminate: C makes the auditee's agreement a condition of the criteria, and D borrows peers' averages instead of this organization's approved tolerance.
Final two: B beats A because the approved tolerance fits this use, while a public benchmark measures performance on the vendor's general data.
Exam cue: the auditor chooses audit criteria from approved tolerances, policy and recognized frameworks. A vendor's benchmark is an input, not a criterion.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Building an audit AI tool
questions.question: The IS audit function fine-tuned and validated a language model to review a Moldovan bank's model documentation, using documents the data science team had rated complete. What is the GREATEST concern with relying on it?

options.A: The tool learned the auditee's own view of complete documentation
options.B: Auditors may accept the tool's summaries without reading the documents
options.C: The tool runs on the bank's servers instead of a vendor's cloud
options.D: The tool was fine-tuned from an existing model, not built from scratch

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool trained on labels the auditee wrote learns the auditee's judgment, so its reviews are not objective evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool learned from and who produced it.
questions.correct_explanation: A fine-tuned model learns its standard from its labels, and here the labels are the data science team's ratings of its own work. Validating on more of those ratings only shows the tool agrees with the team, so its reviews echo the auditee, not the audit criteria. Over-reliance is a real risk, but review rules can manage it; they cannot remove a bias built into the labels.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automation bias is a known risk of AI tools. But review rules can manage it; labels written by the auditee bias every review the tool makes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hosting choices affect risk. But in-house hosting keeps data inside the bank; it does not make the tool's output less reliable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a custom build sounds more rigorous. But fine-tuning an existing model is normal practice; the training labels, not the build method, set what the tool accepts.

tips: Eliminate: D treats fine-tuning as a weakness, and C treats in-house hosting as one; neither decides whether the reviews are objective.
Final two: A beats B because review rules can manage over-reliance, but a tool trained on the auditee's own ratings repeats the auditee's judgment.
Exam cue: an AI tool learns its standard from its training labels. If the auditee wrote the labels, the tool reviews with the auditee's eyes.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Approving an audit AI use
questions.question: An audit team's approved generative AI tool will read supplier invoices and contracts, uploaded by an Egyptian cement producer's procurement staff, to flag possible kickbacks. Which risk should the chief audit executive weigh MOST heavily?

options.A: The tool may flag many innocent invoices as possible kickbacks
options.B: Auditors may need training before writing prompts for the tool
options.C: The vendor may train its models on the documents the tool reads
options.D: Planted text in the documents could make the tool skip items

questions.key_concept: Audit AI tools that read auditee-controlled content can be steered by planted instructions, silently hiding evidence; weigh this before approving the use.
questions.pre_read: Ask who wrote the documents the tool will read and what they would want it to miss.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool can treat text it reads as instructions. Here suppliers wrote the files and procurement staff, whose dealings are under review, upload them, so anyone hiding kickbacks could cheaply plant wording that tells the tool to pass over items, and the audit would never see them. False flags are likely too, but they are visible and get followed up; steered misses are silent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because false flags waste audit effort. But they are visible and followed up; items the tool is steered to skip are never seen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because prompting is a new skill. But training is easily arranged and does not stop the documents themselves steering the tool.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors may reuse inputs. But the tool is approved, so its data terms were already assessed before this use.

tips: Eliminate: C reopens data terms the tool's approval already covered, and B is a training gap that is easily closed.
Final two: D beats A because false flags are visible and followed up, while planted text can silently hide the very items under audit.
Exam cue: when an audit AI tool reads content the auditee controls, weigh indirect prompt injection. The auditee could steer the audit's own tool.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. AI-assisted risk ranking
questions.question: A Bolivian remittance firm's audit team trained a model on eight years of outlet audit findings to rank its 220 outlets; audits in that time reached about half of them. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model may rank never-audited outlets as low risk
options.B: The model may need retraining as each year's outlet findings arrive
options.C: The audit team built the model rather than the data science team
options.D: The model's rankings are harder to explain than a weighted risk score

questions.key_concept: A model trained on past audit findings learns where audits went, not where risk is; never-audited areas look low risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the training data records and what it could never contain.
questions.correct_explanation: A model learns only from the data it is given. Outlets never audited have no findings, so the model can read that silence as low risk and keep steering audits back to outlets already visited, a feedback loop that leaves about half the network unexamined. Explainability matters for presenting the plan, but a clear explanation of this ranking would still carry the same blind spot.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining adds work. But regular retraining is routine upkeep, and new findings come only from outlets that audits reach, so it cannot fill the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data scientists know modeling. But audit building its own analytics supports independence; who built it does not create the blind spot.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee must understand the plan. But explanation tools can help; even a clearly explained ranking inherits the blind spot in its data.

tips: Eliminate: B treats routine retraining as a risk, and C questions who built the model, which supports rather than weakens independence.
Final two: A beats D because absent findings mean absent audits, not low risk; a clear explanation of a skewed ranking still misses half the outlets.
Exam cue: when AI learns from past audit results, ask what the data never captured. Areas never examined look clean to a model.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing reviewer judgment
questions.question: A Nigerian exam council's model flags answer sheets for suspected cheating, and examiners confirm or clear each flag. Which test gives the IS auditor the BEST evidence that examiners judge flags independently?

options.A: Interview examiners about how they weigh flagged answer sheets
options.B: Recompute the model's false-flag rate from the examiners' decisions
options.C: Compare each examiner's clearance rate with the council-wide average
options.D: Seed clean answer sheets into the flag queue and record each decision

questions.key_concept: Seeded known-answer cases test whether human reviewers catch AI errors, exposing shared automation bias that comparing reviewers can miss.
questions.pre_read: Ask which test would show a wrong flag being caught, not just a decision being recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: Automation bias shows when reviewers accept a model's output without real judgment. Seeding clean answer sheets, set up with the council so that no student is affected, works like an integrated test facility: it tests directly whether examiners clear wrong flags. Comparing each examiner's clearance rate with the council-wide average finds outliers, but if every examiner defers to the model alike, every rate looks typical and no wrong flag is exposed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because examiners can describe their judgment. But inquiry gives their account, not evidence that they clear wrong flags in practice.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it uses every decision. But it treats the examiners' decisions as the truth, which is exactly what is in doubt.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it covers every examiner. But comparing rates shows outliers, not accuracy; if all examiners defer to the model, every rate looks normal.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on the examiners' own account, and B treats their decisions as the truth when their judgment is what is being tested.
Final two: D beats C because known-answer cases measure whether examiners catch wrong flags; rates only compare examiners who may all defer alike.
Exam cue: to test whether reviewers really judge AI output, use cases whose right answer is known. Comparing reviewers with each other cannot reveal bias they all share.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing an output filter
questions.question: A Uruguayan children's learning app uses an output filter to stop its tutoring chatbot from showing unsuitable content. Which procedure gives the IS auditor the BEST evidence that the filter operates effectively?

options.A: Inspect the filter's configured block lists and moderation rules
options.B: Count the replies the filter blocked in each month this year
options.C: Send reworded and disguised prompts and inspect the replies
options.D: Read the filter vendor's description of how its filter works

questions.key_concept: AI guardrails are tested by attempting bypasses, such as reworded or disguised prompts; counts of blocked outputs cannot reveal misses.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence could show content that got past the filter.
questions.correct_explanation: Filters can often be bypassed by rewording a request or hiding it inside another task, so only trying such prompts shows whether unsuitable content gets through. Run in a test environment agreed with management, the test measures misses directly. Monthly block counts show the filter is active, but they cannot show what it let through, which is the risk to children.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because block lists define the filter. But configuration shows design, not whether reworded prompts can bypass it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because logs show the filter working all year. But blocked replies count catches; content that got through never appears in the count.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors document their products. But a description is the vendor's claim, not evidence of how the filter performs here.

tips: Eliminate: A inspects design rather than operation, and D relies on the vendor's description instead of evidence.
Final two: C beats B because block counts record only catches, while reworded and disguised prompts reveal what gets through.
Exam cue: to test an AI guardrail, try to get past it the way users would. Counts of blocked items never show the misses.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Sampling over an audit period
questions.question: An Argentine labor court retrained its case-priority model three times during the year under audit; one version ran three weeks. Which change to a random sample of 60 decisions BEST supports the IS auditor's conclusion?

options.A: Stratify the sample by the model version that made each decision
options.B: Rely on each version's validation report instead of sampling
options.C: Draw the 60 decisions from the current model version
options.D: Stratify the sample by the priority level each decision assigned

questions.key_concept: Each retraining creates a new model; a period conclusion needs every version represented, so stratify AI samples by model version.
questions.pre_read: Count how many models actually made the year's decisions and how many cases each would get.
questions.correct_explanation: Each retraining produces a different model, so a conclusion on the year needs evidence on every version that decided. A random sample of 60 would hold only about three decisions from the three-week version, too few to say anything about it; stratifying by version guarantees enough from each. Stratifying by priority looks rigorous, but its strata ignore the retrainings, so the short-lived version can still get almost no cases.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because validation reports describe each version. But they are builders' pre-release tests, not evidence of how each version decided real cases.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the current version is the one still deciding. But the conclusion covers the year, and earlier versions made most of its decisions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because stratifying by outcome is common. But priority strata ignore the retrainings, so the three-week version can still get almost no cases.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps production decisions for builders' pre-release reports, and C covers only today's version when a conclusion on the year needs every version.
Final two: A beats D because each retraining makes a new model; strata by priority can still leave the three-week version almost untested.
Exam cue: when a model changed during the period, treat each version as its own population and sample each one.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Strata for a scoring model
questions.question: A Bulgarian power distributor's model sends inspectors to meters scoring above 0.8 for suspected tampering. To estimate how many of its flags are wrong, which stratum is MOST useful for the IS auditor to add?

options.A: Flagged meters at the households with the highest bills
options.B: Flagged meters that scored just above the 0.8 cut-off
options.C: Flagged meters whose tampering scores were 0.95 or higher
options.D: Unflagged meters that scored just below the 0.8 cut-off

questions.key_concept: Among a model's flags, those just above the cut-off are the closest calls; a stratum there estimates wrong flags better than value strata.
questions.pre_read: Match the stratum to the error the objective names: wrong flags, not missed tampering.
questions.correct_explanation: Among flagged meters, those scored just above the cut-off are the closest calls, so wrong flags are most likely there. A stratum there gives the auditor enough of those cases to estimate the false-flag rate. Bill size suits a test of financial exposure, but it says nothing about whether a tampering flag is wrong, and the objective is wrongful flags on households.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because auditors often stratify by value. But bill size does not track model error; the objective is how many of the model's flags are wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because high scores look like clear cases. But they are the flags least likely to be wrong, so they reveal little about the false-flag rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because near-misses also sit by the cut-off. But unflagged meters show missed tampering, while the objective is households flagged wrongly.

tips: Eliminate: C samples the flags least likely to be wrong, and D tests misses when the objective is wrongful flags.
Final two: B beats A because wrong flags gather just above the cut-off, while bill size measures money, not the model's mistakes.
Exam cue: to find an AI model's wrong flags, sample just above its cut-off score, where the calls are closest.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reported model accuracy
questions.question: A Rwandan coffee exporter's model owner reports that its farm-credit model is 92% accurate, measured on repayments by the farms it approved. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern with this evidence?

options.A: The predictions may come from several versions of the model
options.B: Repayment data may arrive months after each farm's credit decision
options.C: The owner, not an independent party, calculated the figure
options.D: It cannot show how many rejected farms would have repaid

questions.key_concept: When outcomes are recorded only for approved cases, accuracy cannot measure wrongful rejections, a key limit of AI performance evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask which applicants ever get an outcome recorded, and which errors that leaves unmeasured.
questions.correct_explanation: Repayments exist only for farms the model approved, so the 92% describes approvals alone. It cannot show how many rejected farms would have repaid, the error that turns good farmers away. The owner's figure does need independent recomputation, but an auditor recomputing from the same records would inherit the same blind spot, because outcomes for rejected farms were never observed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because each version is a different model. But results can be split by version; missing outcomes for rejected farms cannot be recovered.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because late outcomes delay testing. But timing can be handled with older decisions; it never yields outcomes for rejected farms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because self-reported metrics need recomputing. But an independent recomputation on these records shares the blind spot; rejected farms have no outcomes.

tips: Eliminate: A can be handled by splitting results by version, and B is a timing issue that older decisions solve.
Final two: D beats C because independent recomputation on the same records would share the blind spot; rejected farms never get outcomes.
Exam cue: when a model's decisions control which outcomes get recorded, accuracy on those outcomes cannot show wrongful rejections.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. AI-graded full population
questions.question: An IS auditor plans to have a second large language model grade all 40,000 answers a Sri Lankan rail operator's ticketing chatbot gave last quarter. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Use the chatbot's own underlying model as the grader
options.B: Ask the chatbot's vendor to review the grader's marking approach
options.C: Compare the grader's marks with expert grading on a sample of answers
options.D: Plan to report each answer the grader marks wrong as an exception

questions.key_concept: An AI grader used for full-population testing must be validated against expert judgment first; the audited model cannot grade itself.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the auditor would know whether the grader's marks are right.
questions.correct_explanation: A grader model is an audit tool, so it needs validation before reliance: comparing its marks with expert grading on a sample measures how often it is wrong, in both directions. Reporting every answer it marks wrong would give full coverage, but an unvalidated grader's marks are leads: some flagged answers may be right, and some wrong answers may pass unmarked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the same model knows the chatbot's style. But it shares the chatbot's blind spots and would tend to pass its own wrong answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor understands the chatbot. But the vendor is not independent of the answers being graded, and reviewing an approach is not validation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because full coverage finds every error. But an unvalidated grader's marks are leads; each needs follow-up before it is an exception.

tips: Eliminate: A makes the audited chatbot's own model grade its answers, and B asks a party tied to the chatbot to vouch for the test.
Final two: C beats D because an unvalidated grader's marks are leads, not exceptions; expert-graded samples show how far its marks can be trusted.
Exam cue: an AI that grades another AI is an audit tool. Validate it against expert judgment before relying on its marks.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Evidence for a past chatbot answer
questions.question: A Barbadian insurer's chatbot told a customer on March 3 that flood damage was excluded; the chatbot has been updated repeatedly since. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor what governed that answer?

options.A: The chatbot's current system prompt and configuration settings
options.B: The March 3 chat log with the prompt version then in force
options.C: The model version log showing which model ran on March 3
options.D: The chatbot team's account of how it answered on March 3

questions.key_concept: A chatbot's system prompt is configuration that shapes its answers; evidence about a past answer needs the prompt version then in force.
questions.pre_read: Note the date of the answer and what has changed since. Ask which records show the setup live that day.
questions.correct_explanation: A chatbot's answers depend on its system prompt, the insurer's instructions on what to say, not just on the base model, and the chatbot has changed since March 3. The chat log shows what was said, and the prompt version in force that day, from the change history, shows what governed it. The model version for that day is relevant, but it cannot show the insurer's instructions.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is the system's own configuration. But it reflects later edits; the prompt that shaped the March 3 answer may no longer be live.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it matches the date. But a model version shows which model ran, not the insurer's instructions that shaped the answer about coverage.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the team knows the chatbot. But an account is inquiry and cannot show which instructions were live on March 3.

tips: Eliminate: A shows today's prompt after later edits, and D relies on the team's account instead of records.
Final two: B beats C because the insurer's prompt shapes what the chatbot says about coverage; a model version log cannot show the instructions live on March 3.
Exam cue: for generative AI, prompts and settings are configuration. Match the evidence to the prompt version live when the output was produced, not only the model.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Red-team report as evidence
questions.question: To show that a Hong Kong broker's research assistant resists prompt injection, the model owner gives the IS auditor an independent firm's red-team report predating the assistant's model upgrade. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Find out what the upgrade changed and whether it was retested
options.B: Ask the model owner to confirm the upgrade did not weaken security
options.C: Request the vendor's own red-team results for the new base model
options.D: Rely on the report because an independent firm carried it out

questions.key_concept: AI test evidence, such as red-team results, applies to the model version tested; after an upgrade, confirm what changed and what was retested.
questions.pre_read: Compare the date of the evidence with the date of the last model change.
questions.correct_explanation: Red-team results describe the version tested. A model upgrade can change how the assistant responds to injected instructions, so the report may no longer reflect what runs today. The auditor first learns what changed and whether testing was repeated. An independent firm adds objectivity, but independence does not make evidence about an earlier model current.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the model owner knows the change. But a confirmation is the owner's assertion, not evidence of how the new model behaves.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor tested the new model. But vendor tests cover its base model, not this assistant's prompts, data and connections.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because independent testing is strong evidence. But it tested the earlier model; independence does not carry results over to the upgrade.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts the owner's assertion, and C relies on vendor tests of the base model rather than this deployment.
Final two: A beats D because AI test evidence holds only for the version tested; an independent report on an earlier model is out of date.
Exam cue: tie every AI test report to the model version it covers. An upgrade or retraining can void earlier results.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Hosted assistant logs
questions.question: An IS auditor will test six months of answers from a Greek hospital group's vendor-hosted patient assistant, but the vendor deletes chat logs after 30 days. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask management to suspend the assistant until logging is changed
options.B: Recreate earlier answers by asking the assistant the same questions again
options.C: Have the model owner preserve current logs and any earlier records
options.D: Treat the last 30 days of logs as the six-month population

questions.key_concept: Hosted AI logs may expire under vendor settings; the auditor asks the model owner to preserve them, since rerunning cannot recreate past outputs.
questions.pre_read: Compare the audit period with how long the records exist.
questions.correct_explanation: Logs are the evidence of what the assistant told patients, and the vendor's 30-day deletion keeps destroying them. Having the model owner preserve them now, under the hospital's privacy rules, stops further loss, and earlier records that remain, such as exports or complaint files, show what the earlier months can still support. Asking the same questions again produces new answers from today's version and settings, not the answers patients received.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it stops unlogged answers. But suspending a patient service to suit the audit puts audit convenience ahead of patients; preserving the evidence meets the audit's need.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems to rebuild the record. But generative answers vary between runs and versions; new answers do not show what patients were told.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because recent logs are available. But 30 days cannot stand for six months, and narrowing the period without saying so misstates the scope.

tips: Eliminate: D presents 30 days as the six-month population, and A suspends a patient service for the audit's convenience when preserving evidence is enough.
Final two: C beats B because asking again produces fresh answers from today's model; only preserved records show what patients were told.
Exam cue: for hosted AI, check the provider's log retention early. Preserve evidence before it expires; never recreate past outputs by rerunning.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An assistant's statement about itself
questions.question: Asked during fieldwork, a Luxembourg private bank's vendor-hosted staff assistant replies that it deletes every prompt immediately. How should the IS auditor BEST treat this reply?

options.A: Rely on it as system-generated evidence of the retention practice
options.B: Verify it against the service contract and retention configuration
options.C: Rely on it if the assistant can quote the vendor's privacy policy
options.D: Confirm it against the vendor's published model card for the assistant

questions.key_concept: An AI assistant's statements about its own behavior are generated text, not system records; verify them against contracts and configuration.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the reply is a record of the setup or text the model produced.
questions.correct_explanation: A language model's answer about itself is generated text, not a record of how the service is set up, and it can be confidently wrong. Retention is fixed by the service contract and the configuration, so those are the evidence. A model card is a vendor document, but it describes the model's design and limits, not this bank's contract terms or retention settings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because system output usually outranks inquiry. But a chatbot's reply is generated text, not a system record, and can be confidently wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a quoted policy sounds documented. But the assistant can misquote or invent a policy, and a policy is not the bank's contract or settings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is the vendor's own documentation. But a model card describes the model, not this deployment's contract or retention settings.

tips: Eliminate: A treats generated text as a system record, and C trusts a quotation the assistant itself generates.
Final two: B beats D because retention is set by the contract and configuration; a model card describes the model, not this deployment.
Exam cue: what an AI system says about itself is a claim to verify. Look for the records and settings that actually govern it.
