questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. AI-listed requirements
questions.question: An IS auditor asked a generative AI tool to list the data-protection rules that apply to a client's patient-triage chatbot; it returned 14 requirements, each citing an article number. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Adopt the 14 requirements and their article numbers as audit criteria
options.B: Ask the tool to remove any requirement it is unsure about
options.C: Ask the tool to give a source link for each requirement
options.D: Check each requirement and article against the official legal text

questions.key_concept: Generative AI can confabulate citations; requirements it lists must be verified against official texts before they become audit criteria.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool's citations rest on and where the auditor can confirm them.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative tools can invent rules and article numbers that look exact, so the list is a lead, not criteria. Checking each item against the official text confirms that it exists and says what the tool claims before it shapes the audit. Asking for source links seems to add traceability, but the links are generated too and may be wrong; they still have to be opened and checked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because article numbers look authoritative. But a tool can invent precise-looking citations, and unverified criteria could misdirect the whole audit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems to filter out weak items. But a model's sense of its own certainty is unreliable; confident errors would stay in the list.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because links seem to make each item traceable. But generated links can be wrong or invented, and they still need to be opened and checked.

tips: Eliminate: A treats confident citations as proof, and B relies on the tool judging its own certainty.
Final two: D beats C because only the official text confirms a rule; generated links are more output that still needs checking.
Exam cue: generative AI can invent citations. Verify any law, standard or clause it names against the source before using it.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Checking extracted data
questions.question: An approved AI tool extracted weights from 8,000 scanned Ghanaian cocoa delivery notes and scored its confidence in each; the IS auditor plans to check only extractions below 90%. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Extractions scored 90% or above can be wrong and go unchecked
options.B: Extractions below 90% may be mostly right, wasting checking effort
options.C: Handwritten notes may get lower confidence scores than printed ones
options.D: The 90% cut-off came from the auditor rather than the tool's vendor

questions.key_concept: AI confidence scores are self-estimates; using them to skip verification leaves confident errors untested in audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask which errors the checking plan could never find.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's confidence score is its own estimate, and models can be confidently wrong, for example on unfamiliar layouts. Checking only low scores leaves high-confidence errors untested, and they flow straight into the audit evidence. Low-scored items that prove correct only cost time. The auditor should also test a sample of high-confidence extractions to measure their error rate.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wasted effort is a real cost. But extra checks only cost time; unchecked high-confidence errors enter the evidence unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because handwriting is harder to read. But lower scores send those notes to checking; the risk lies in errors scored high.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors know their tools. But a vendor default is no more validated for these notes than the auditor's choice.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes a vendor default would be validated, and C describes items that the plan already sends for checking.
Final two: A beats B because extra checks only waste time, while confident errors pass into the evidence untested.
Exam cue: an AI confidence score is the model's self-estimate, not proof. Test a sample of high-confidence output too.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI-assisted access review
questions.question: An IS auditor gave an approved AI assistant a Cypriot shipping line's leavers list and 60,000-line access export, several times its context window; it named 12 active leaver accounts. What should the auditor verify FIRST?

options.A: That the vendor's terms bar it from training on the export
options.B: That the prompt and the assistant's version are saved in work papers
options.C: That the assistant's result covers all 60,000 exported lines
options.D: That each of the 12 named accounts stayed active after departure

questions.key_concept: An AI assistant given more than its context window can silently process only part; the auditor confirms completeness before relying on the result.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the answer covers every record or only the records the tool read.
questions.correct_explanation: A context window is the amount of input an assistant can process at once. Given more, assistants can silently read only part, then answer as if they saw everything. Reconciling the lines it processed to the 60,000 shows whether the 12 come from the whole population; if not, the test is rerun in batches that fit. Confirming the 12 is needed too, but it cannot reveal leavers in lines never read.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because audit data must stay confidential. But the assistant is approved, so its data terms were already assessed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because documentation supports review. But saving the prompt records what was asked; it does not show whether every line was read.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because each named account must be confirmed before reporting. But that tests the hits; leavers in unread lines would stay invisible.

tips: Eliminate: B documents the work without testing it, and A reopens data terms the approval already covered.
Final two: C beats D because confirming the 12 tests only what was found; if lines went unread, the result cannot support a conclusion on the whole population.
Exam cue: before trusting an AI tool's answer about a population, reconcile what it actually processed to the source record count. Its own claim of full coverage is not evidence.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Regional pricing test
questions.question: Testing whether a Romanian lender priced borrowers fairly across regions, an IS auditor finds 6% of loans missing from the pricing model's log: timeouts priced by a fixed rule. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Proceed with the logged loans and record the 6% gap as immaterial
options.B: Add the rule-priced loans from the loan system to the population
options.C: Have the model owner rerun the timed-out requests through the model now
options.D: Limit the population to loans that the model itself priced

questions.key_concept: An AI decision population includes fallback decisions made when the model fails; define the population by the audit objective.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the objective is about the model's outputs or the outcomes people received.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is whether borrowers were priced fairly, and the fallback rule priced 6% of them, so those loans belong in the population. Timeouts may not fall evenly across regions, so leaving them out could hide the very pattern under test. Excluding them would suit a test of the model alone, but this objective covers every borrower's rate, including those the fallback set.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the gap looks small. But a gap with a known cause may be concentrated in some regions, so it cannot be assumed immaterial.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it fills the gap with model prices. But rerun prices are not the rates borrowers got, and today's model may differ.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model did not set those rates. But the objective is how borrowers were priced, and the fallback rule priced those borrowers.

tips: Eliminate: C creates prices borrowers never received, and A accepts a known population gap without testing whether it matters.
Final two: B beats D because the objective is how borrowers were priced, and the fixed rule priced those borrowers; dropping them could hide a regional pattern.
Exam cue: an AI system's population includes its fallback path. Define it by the objective, not by which component decided.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Minutes-review tool
questions.question: An Omani group's audit team checked an AI tool that finds related-party dealings in English board minutes and now wants to use it on Arabic minutes. What should the chief audit executive require FIRST?

options.A: Rerunning the English test cases to show the tool is unchanged
options.B: Follow-up of every dealing the tool flags in Arabic minutes
options.C: Machine translation of the minutes into English before using the tool
options.D: Testing on Arabic minutes whose dealings are already known

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's validation applies only to data like that tested; a new language or data type needs revalidation before reliance.
questions.pre_read: Compare the data the tool was validated on with the data it will now read.
questions.correct_explanation: A validation holds only for data like the data tested. Unlike a fixed audit program, an AI tool's accuracy shifts with the data it reads, and Arabic minutes differ in language, wording and layout, so error rates on them are unknown until it is tested on Arabic minutes with known answers. Translating into English seems to reuse the validation, but translation adds its own errors, and the tool was never validated on translated text either.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an unchanged audit program keeps its earlier testing. But an AI tool's accuracy depends on the data it reads; English results say nothing about Arabic minutes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because flags get checked. But follow-up finds false flags only; dealings the tool misses in Arabic are never seen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it routes minutes to the validated setting. But translation adds errors, and the tool was never validated on translated text.

tips: Eliminate: A retests the unchanged tool on English, which says nothing about Arabic, and B checks flags while misses go unseen.
Final two: D beats C because translation adds its own errors; only known-answer testing on Arabic minutes shows how the tool performs.
Exam cue: an AI audit tool's validation covers the data it was tested on. New languages, formats or sources need revalidation.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Anomaly tool reliance
questions.question: An audit team wants to rely on an anomaly-detection tool for a Botswanan trucking firm's fuel-card transactions, but no past cases with known answers exist. Which approach BEST supports that reliance?

options.A: Run the tool and follow up every transaction it flags
options.B: Run a second anomaly tool and compare the two sets of flags
options.C: Plant synthetic anomalies in a data copy and measure what is found
options.D: Rely on the detection rate the tool's vendor reports for fuel-card fraud

questions.key_concept: When no known-outcome data exists, seeded synthetic anomalies let the auditor measure an AI tool's miss rate before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the team could learn what the tool misses.
questions.correct_explanation: Validation needs cases whose answers are known. When none exist, planting realistic synthetic anomalies in a copy of the data creates them, and the share the tool finds estimates its miss rate. Following up every flag is necessary, but it measures only false alarms; anomalies the tool never flags stay invisible, so it cannot show how far the tool can be relied on.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every flag gets tested. But follow-up reveals false alarms only; anomalies the tool misses are never seen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because two tools seem to check each other. But tools can share blind spots; agreement is not a measured miss rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor figures sound objective. But they come from other data, not this firm's fuel-card transactions.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on vendor figures from other data, and B treats agreement between tools as accuracy.
Final two: C beats A because planted anomalies reveal what the tool misses; following up flags shows only its false alarms.
Exam cue: if no known outcomes exist, create them. Seeded test cases let the auditor measure an AI tool's misses before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI platform in an investigation
questions.question: Investigating suspected procurement fraud in a Trinidadian ministry's IT unit, the IS audit team may use that unit's AI platform, which keeps no copy of analyzed emails. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The platform runs an open-source model rather than a major vendor's
options.B: Platform administrators can see the team's prompts and outputs
options.C: The platform's model has not been validated for analyzing emails
options.D: The platform's model is smaller than the leading public models

questions.key_concept: AI platforms log prompts and outputs; using one the auditee controls can expose confidential audit work and undermine independence.
questions.pre_read: Ask who runs the platform and what they could see.
questions.correct_explanation: AI platforms log prompts and outputs, and their administrators can usually read them. Keeping no copy of the emails does not change that. Here the administrators work in the unit under investigation, so they could see which people and payments the auditors are examining, defeating the investigation's confidentiality and independence. Validation matters before relying on any tool, but it cannot fix who runs the platform.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because some assume open-source models are less trustworthy. But a model's origin does not decide reliability; validation and who controls the platform do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an unvalidated tool is unreliable. But validation could be arranged; testing cannot fix a platform run by the people under investigation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because bigger models often perform better. But size does not decide fitness for this task, and it does not touch the confidentiality problem.

tips: Eliminate: A judges the model by its origin and D by its size; neither decides reliability or confidentiality.
Final two: B beats C because testing could fix an unvalidated model, but not operators under investigation who can see the auditors' prompts.
Exam cue: an AI tool's prompt logs reveal what the auditor is examining. Keep confidential audit work off platforms the auditee controls.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A rerun that differs
questions.question: An IS auditor reran last year's AI extraction of refund amounts from 4,000 letters using recorded settings, prompts and input; 3% differ, as the vendor retired the original version. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the vendor to restore the retired version for one rerun
options.B: Replace last year's amounts with the newer version's results
options.C: Keep last year's amounts and document the recorded run conditions
options.D: Check the differing amounts against the source and record the results

questions.key_concept: Recorded conditions make an AI rerun explainable, not guaranteed; when results differ, the auditor verifies against source records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the records explain and what only the source data can settle.
questions.correct_explanation: Hosted models change, so even a well-recorded rerun can differ. The records explain why, a different version, but not which amounts are right. Checking the differing amounts against the source letters shows whether last year's results held, and recording that outcome settles the question. Keeping last year's amounts because conditions were recorded mistakes documentation for verification: recording makes a difference explainable, not correct.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the old version would reproduce the original. But vendors seldom restore retired versions, and a matching rerun still would not show the amounts are right.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the newer version is current. But it is a different model, and its amounts are no more verified than last year's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recording conditions is good practice. But records explain why results differ; only the source letters show which amounts are right.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps one unverified result for another, and A depends on the vendor reviving a retired version.
Final two: D beats C because recorded conditions explain a difference but cannot settle it; the source letters can.
Exam cue: hosted AI cannot always be rerun exactly. When a rerun differs, go back to the source records rather than to either output.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Recommending on a biased model
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that an Austrian bank's voice-authentication model locks out customers with speech impairments far more often than other customers. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner set group lockout limits and fix any breach
options.B: Have the model owner raise the model's overall accuracy target
options.C: Retrain the model on 2,000 hours of speech from affected customers
options.D: Tell customers in the app that voice checks may sometimes fail

questions.key_concept: AI recommendations set group-level outcomes for a named owner; overall accuracy targets can hide a small group's harm, and owners choose the fix.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each proposed measure would reveal the affected group's results, and who designs the fix.
questions.correct_explanation: An overall accuracy figure is dominated by the largest group, so a higher target can be met while customers with speech impairments stay locked out. Lockout limits for each group, owned and acted on by the model owner, make the gap visible and hold someone to closing it. The auditor recommends that outcome and its owner; the owner chooses the technical fix.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because better accuracy sounds like the cure. But an average can rise while a small group's lockouts stay high, so the gap could persist unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more representative data often narrows such gaps. But designing the fix is the owner's job; the auditor recommends the result to achieve.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is transparent. But a notice leaves affected customers locked out; it informs without fixing anything.

tips: Eliminate: C has the auditor designing the model fix, and D informs customers without reducing lockouts.
Final two: A beats B because an overall target can be met while one group stays locked out; group limits make the gap visible and owned.
Exam cue: AI recommendations name a measurable outcome for each affected group and an owner. Averages hide small groups, and the fix is the owner's.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Reporting a wait-time gap
questions.question: A Welsh council's AI policy requires fairness criteria for every model, but its repair-priority model has none, and Welsh-language requests wait 40% longer. How should the IS auditor BEST report this?

options.A: Report the wait gap as a finding against an auditor-set limit
options.B: Report nothing until the model owner has set fairness criteria
options.C: Report the missing fairness criteria, with the wait gap as effect
options.D: Report the wait gap as unlawful discrimination against Welsh speakers

questions.key_concept: If required AI fairness criteria are missing, the auditor reports the policy breach with its effect; model owners, not auditors, set fairness thresholds.
questions.pre_read: Find the criterion that already exists and the one that is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy is the criterion, and the condition is that the model has no fairness criteria. With no limit to measure it against, the 40% gap cannot be called a breach, but it shows what the missing control allows: the effect on Welsh-language residents. Setting a limit and reporting a breach would have the auditor define the model's fairness threshold, a job for the model owner within senior management's tolerances.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a finding against a number looks concrete. But turning fairness into a measurable limit is the model owner's job; an auditor-set limit would impair independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because there is no threshold to measure against. But the policy itself is the criterion, and its breach is reportable now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the gap affects one language group. But unlawfulness is a legal judgment; the auditor reports facts against criteria and can refer possible breaches of language duties to counsel.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for criteria when the policy already supplies one, and D reaches a legal conclusion the auditor cannot make.
Final two: C beats A because the missing criteria breach the policy; setting a limit for the model would put the auditor in the model owner's role.
Exam cue: when an AI model lacks required criteria, report the governance gap against policy. Setting the model's fairness threshold is the model owner's job, not the auditor's.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Explaining a model metric
questions.question: An IS auditor must explain to the audit committee that a Nepali health ministry's tuberculosis screening model has a false-negative rate three times higher in mountain districts. Which presentation is BEST?

options.A: How many healthy people it wrongly flags in mountain districts
options.B: How many sick people it likely misses, and the consequences
options.C: The model's overall accuracy across every district
options.D: The retraining method the IS auditor would use to close the gap

questions.key_concept: Explain technical AI findings to boards in terms of harm: a false-negative rate becomes real cases missed and their consequences.
questions.pre_read: Translate the metric into what happens to people before choosing a format.
questions.correct_explanation: A false-negative rate means sick people the model fails to flag. Committee members act on consequences, so the auditor translates the rate into the estimated number of people missed in mountain districts and what follows for them, such as later treatment. An overall accuracy figure looks balanced, but it blends all districts and can hide the mountain districts' gap, the harm the finding is about.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because wrong flags also harm people. But those are false positives; a false negative is a sick person the model fails to flag.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an overall figure gives context. But it blends all districts, so it can hide the mountain districts' missed cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a fix seems helpful. But designing the retraining is management's job, and the committee needs the risk, not a method.

tips: Eliminate: A describes false positives, not the false negatives in the finding, and D has the auditor designing the model fix.
Final two: B beats C because an overall figure blends all districts and can hide the gap; the committee needs the cases missed and what follows.
Exam cue: report AI metrics in terms of people and the business. A false-negative rate becomes the number of real cases missed.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Closing a drift finding
questions.question: An IS auditor reported that a Latvian online retailer's returns-fraud model had no drift monitoring; at follow-up, management shows the retrained model is accurate again. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the restored accuracy as evidence the drift finding is resolved
options.B: Retest accuracy on a sample of decisions since the retraining
options.C: Review the retrained model's validation report and monitoring plan
options.D: Verify that drift monitoring with alert limits and an owner now operates

questions.key_concept: Follow-up on an AI finding verifies that the missing control now operates; a retrained model's restored accuracy treats only the symptom.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the finding said was missing, then ask what management has shown.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding was missing drift monitoring; restored accuracy fixes the symptom, and drift can recur as customers' return patterns change. Follow-up verifies that the agreed control now operates: alert limits set, alerts reaching an owner and responses recorded. Retesting recent decisions is strong evidence of today's accuracy, but it does not show that the next decline will be detected.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the metric is back in range. But the cause was missing monitoring; without it, the next decline will again go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because production retests are strong follow-up evidence. But they show today's accuracy, the symptom; the finding was missing monitoring, which a retest does not examine.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it shows testing and intent. But a report and a plan show design; follow-up needs evidence that monitoring operates.

tips: Eliminate: A closes on a restored metric while the cause remains, and C offers a plan and a pre-release report, which show only design.
Final two: D beats B because the finding was missing monitoring; a production retest shows today's accuracy, not that the next decline will be caught.
Exam cue: follow-up tests what the finding reported. When it reported a missing control, retraining fixes only the symptom; close it when that control operates.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Defending an AI-assisted finding
questions.question: Czech hospital managers dispute a finding that 312 overtime claims cover hours when badge records show staff off-site, calling the IS auditor's AI matching tool a black box. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Walk the managers through the badge and claim records for each item
options.B: Show the managers the vendor's accuracy certificate for the tool
options.C: Rerun the matching tool on the badge and claim records with managers
options.D: Withdraw the finding until the tool's method can be explained

questions.key_concept: AI tools find leads, but findings rest on source evidence the auditor verified and can show, so accountability stays with the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the finding actually rests on: the tool's output or the records behind it.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool found the leads, but the finding rests on records: the badge logs and the overtime claims for each item. Walking managers through that evidence shows the conclusion is the auditor's, supported by sources they can check, with no need to explain the tool's inner workings. Rerunning the tool shows only that it repeats itself; consistency does not show the claims are wrong.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certificates sound authoritative. But a vendor's claim about the tool does not show these 312 claims are wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a repeated result looks convincing. But it shows the tool is consistent, not that its matches are right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because unexplained AI output is weak evidence. But this finding rests on badge and claim records the auditor can show, not on the tool.

tips: Eliminate: B offers a vendor claim instead of evidence, and D withdraws a finding that rests on records rather than on the tool.
Final two: A beats C because the auditor owns the conclusion through the source records; a rerun shows only that the tool repeats itself.
Exam cue: when AI found it, the evidence must still stand without the AI. Defend findings with source records, not with the tool.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Disclosing AI use
questions.question: A chief audit executive's methodology requires reports to disclose material use of AI in the audit. Which use on an IS auditor's recent engagement MOST needs disclosure?

options.A: A grammar tool that polished the wording of the final report
options.B: An AI search tool that gathered public news about the auditee
options.C: An AI tool that chose which transactions the auditors would test
options.D: An AI tool that translated auditee policies the auditors read for context

questions.key_concept: Material AI use, such as selecting what to test, is disclosed because it shaped the evidence; cosmetic or administrative uses are rarely material.
questions.pre_read: Ask which uses changed what evidence the findings rest on.
questions.correct_explanation: Disclosure tells readers how AI shaped the work they rely on. A tool that chose which transactions to test set the audit's coverage and evidence, so readers need to know how it was used, validated and checked by the auditors. Gathering public news informs background research for planning, but no finding rests on it, so it matters far less to readers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it touched the report itself. But polishing wording does not shape the evidence or conclusions readers rely on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it fed the risk assessment. But background news informs planning; no finding rests on it the way findings rest on test selection.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because translation errors could mislead auditors. But these policies were read for context only; no finding rests on the translation.

tips: Eliminate: A polishes wording and D translated background reading; neither shapes the evidence behind the findings.
Final two: C beats B because test selection sets what evidence exists; background news informs planning but supports no finding.
Exam cue: disclose AI use that shaped scope, evidence or conclusions. Administrative and cosmetic uses rarely need it.
